newsitem.title: UK: Sumitomo situations powerless to prevent - Black.
newsitem.headline: Sumitomo situations powerless to prevent - Black.

text.p: The London Metal Exchange (LME) may be unable to draft new controls in order to prevent situations like the Sumitomo Corp copper scandal, Herbert Black, president of American Iron and Metal Co Inc said.

Black said at an American Metal Market luncheon that although the LME could have taken sterner action regarding the backwardation, it was always possible for unscrupulous operators to find a way round the rules.
"If the wrong people are involved they will find a way to break the rules," Black said.

In June, Japan's Sumitomo said it had fired its former head trader Yasuo Hamanaka after he admitted 10 years of unauthorised trading in copper. Sumitomo said its losses, all on the LME, totalled $2.6 billion.
"I am sure that there is another Hamanaka out there - he is probably five years old at the moment," Black added.
Montreal-based scrap trader Black is widely believed to be among those who broke Sumitomo's control of the copper market that saw three months prices peak at $2,715 earlier this year.
He was instrumental in forcing the copper price lower in early May 1996, when he altered his long speculative position on the LME to a net short by selling 90,000 tonnes during one five-minute ring.
But this strategy was not without risk, given the persistence of the backwardation for cash/threes, which soon afterwards flared out to above $300.
Black voiced some criticism of the LME's actions during recent months.

He said that the LME perhaps could have done more to restrict the backwardation and acted sooner. He noted that the LME board is comprised to a large extent by representatives of ring-trading companies.
Nigel Lion, a former trader and past member of the LME committee, said that the LME faced problems in enquiring into a company that was not an LME member and based in a foreign country.
And LME Chief Executive David King said because of the inquiry into the copper market the exchange launched in November 1995, the LME now knows a lot of what was behind the scenes.
However, there were positions in the physical and OTC (over-the-counter) markets that the LME were unable to investigate, King noted.
